Polynomial growth of Bohnenblust–Hille constants on the Hamming cube

Paata Ivanisvili Address: Department of Mathematics, University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA 92697, USA Email address: pivanisv@uci.edu
Abstract.

We prove that the Bohnenblust–Hille constants for Walsh polynomials on the Hamming cube grow at most polynomially in the degree. More precisely, there is an absolute constant KK such that every f:{−1,1}n→ℂf:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\mathbb{C} of degree at most mm satisfies

(∑|S|≤m|f^​(S)|2​m/(m+1))(m+1)/(2​m)≤K​m27​‖f‖∞.\left(\sum_{|S|\leq m}|\widehat{f}(S)|^{2m/(m+1)}\right)^{(m+1)/(2m)}\leq Km^{27}\|f\|_{\infty}.

The estimate is uniform in the dimension. The exponent 2727 is not optimized.

Key words and phrases: 
Bohnenblust–Hille inequality, Hamming cube, Walsh polynomials, hypercontractivity, random coordinate partitions

1. Introduction and main results

Let Qn={−1,1}nQ_{n}=\{-1,1\}^{n} be equipped with its uniform probability measure. Every function f:Qn→ℂf:Q_{n}\to\mathbb{C} has the Fourier–Walsh expansion

f⁡(x)=∑S⊆[n]f^​(S)​xS,xS=∏j∈Sxj,f^​(S)=𝔼​f​(x)​xS.f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\widehat{f}(S)x^{S},\qquad x^{S}=\prod_{j\in S}x_{j},\qquad\widehat{f}(S)=\mathbb{E}f(x)x^{S}.

We say that ff has degree at most mm if f^​(S)=0\widehat{f}(S)=0 whenever |S|>m|S|>m. Throughout the paper,

qr=2​rr+1,1qr=12+12​r(r≥1).q_{r}=\frac{2r}{r+1},\qquad\frac{1}{q_{r}}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2r}\qquad(r\geq 1).

The Boolean Bohnenblust–Hille problem asks for the growth, as a function of mm, of the least dimension-independent constant 𝖡m\mathsf{B}_{m} in

(1.1) (∑|S|≤m|f^​(S)|qm)1/qm≤𝖡m​‖f‖∞,deg⁡f≤m.\left(\sum_{|S|\leq m}|\widehat{f}(S)|^{q_{m}}\right)^{1/q_{m}}\leq\mathsf{B}_{m}\|f\|_{\infty},\qquad\deg f\leq m.

The classical Bohnenblust–Hille inequality arose in the solution of Bohr’s absolute convergence problem for Dirichlet series: the largest possible gap between the abscissas of absolute and uniform convergence is 1/21/2 [3]. Its polynomial form relates a coefficient ℓqm\ell_{q_{m}} norm to a supremum norm on a polydisc. The dependence of the inequality on the degree is a central quantitative question. In the complex polynomial setting, Bayart, Pellegrino, and Seoane-Sepúlveda [1] established subexponential estimates of the form exp⁡(O⁡(m​log⁡m))\exp(O(\sqrt{m\log m})). They used these estimates to determine the precise asymptotic behavior of the Bohr radius KnK_{n} of the nn-dimensional polydisc, proving Kn∼(log⁡n)/nK_{n}\sim\sqrt{(\log n)/n} as n→∞n\to\infty [1].

For the Boolean cube, Defant, Mastyło, and Pérez [6] proved the corresponding estimate

(1.2) 𝖡m≤C​exp⁡(c​m​log⁡m)\mathsf{B}_{m}\leq C\exp\!\bigl(c\sqrt{m\log m}\bigr)

with absolute constants C,cC,c.

Eskenazis and Ivanisvili [7] used these constants 𝖡m\mathsf{B}_{m} to learn bounded low-degree functions from a number of uniform random examples logarithmic in the dimension. Related Bohnenblust–Hille inequalities also yield learning bounds for low-degree quantum observables [10].

Recently, in a breakthrough paper, Pellegrino and Teixeira [9] obtained polynomial growth of the Bohnenblust–Hille constants for analytic polynomials on the polydisc. Their argument uses a weighted square function. We adapt this approach to hamming cube {−1,1}n\{-1,1\}^{n}. While approahces are similar there are certain distinctions between these proofs: on the polydisc, adjoining one variable makes a polynomial homogeneous without changing its coefficient or supremum norm. On the cube, this construction does not produce a homogeneous Walsh polynomial, and even a single homogeneous level f=rf^{=r} can have larger supremum norm than ff. We therefore work with all degrees together in the weighted square function S⁡(f)S(f). The random coloring of [9] becomes simpler here: each variable occurs at most once in a Walsh monomial, so a binomial estimate captures, on average, a fixed proportion of every high-degree coefficient sum. Bonami–Beckner hypercontractivity bounds the resulting sums by square functions of coordinate restrictions. The weights then give a contraction at fixed dimension, while Markov’s inequality controls the finitely many low degrees.

Our main result is the following.

Theorem 1.1.

There is an absolute constant K<∞K<\infty such that, for every pair of positive integers m,nm,n with m≤nm\leq n and every f:Qn→ℂf:Q_{n}\to\mathbb{C} of degree at most mm,

(1.3) (∑|S|≤m|f^​(S)|2​m/(m+1))(m+1)/(2​m)≤K​m27​‖f‖∞.\left(\sum_{|S|\leq m}|\widehat{f}(S)|^{2m/(m+1)}\right)^{(m+1)/(2m)}\leq Km^{27}\|f\|_{\infty}.

Equivalently, 𝖡m≤K​m27\mathsf{B}_{m}\leq Km^{27} for every m≥1m\geq 1.

The proof gives the following more structured estimate. Write f=r=∑|S|=rf^​(S)​xSf^{=r}=\sum_{|S|=r}\widehat{f}(S)x^{S} and

𝒮r​(f)=(∑|S|=r|f^​(S)|qr)1/qr.\mathcal{S}_{r}(f)=\left(\sum_{|S|=r}|\widehat{f}(S)|^{q_{r}}\right)^{1/q_{r}}.
Theorem 1.2.

There is an absolute constant K<∞K<\infty such that every polynomial as in Theorem 1.1 satisfies

(1.4) (∑r=1m𝒮r​(f)2r10)1/2≤K​m22​‖f‖∞.\left(\sum_{r=1}^{m}\frac{\mathcal{S}_{r}(f)^{2}}{r^{10}}\right)^{1/2}\leq Km^{22}\|f\|_{\infty}.

In Section 2 we prove the two results together, starting with the coefficient norm in (1.3).

As an application, Theorem 1.2 establishes a special case of the Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture [12], for polynomials whose Fourier coefficients have constant absolute value on each degree level. For a real-valued function ff on QnQ_{n}, write

Var⁡(f)=𝔼​|f−𝔼​f|2=∑S≠∅|f^​(S)|2,Infi⁡(f)=∑S∋i|f^​(S)|2.\operatorname{Var}(f)=\mathbb{E}|f-\mathbb{E}f|^{2}=\sum_{S\neq\varnothing}|\widehat{f}(S)|^{2},\qquad\operatorname{Inf}_{i}(f)=\sum_{S\ni i}|\widehat{f}(S)|^{2}.
Corollary 1.3.

There is an absolute constant c>0c>0 such that, for every 1≤m≤n1\leq m\leq n and every f:Qn→[−1,1]f:Q_{n}\to[-1,1] of degree at most mm satisfying |f^​(S)|=a|S||\widehat{f}(S)|=a_{|S|} for some a0,…,am≥0a_{0},\ldots,a_{m}\geq 0 and all |S|≤m|S|\leq m,

Infi⁡(f)≥cm54​Var⁡(f)2for every ​i∈[n].\operatorname{Inf}_{i}(f)\geq\frac{c}{m^{54}}\operatorname{Var}(f)^{2}\qquad\text{for every }i\in[n].

The assumption concerns only the magnitudes of the coefficients; their signs may vary within each level. The proof of Corollary 1.3 is given in Section 3.

The class of polynomials of degree at most mm is stable under freezing coordinates. Every resulting function still has degree at most mm and supremum norm at most 11. A function of fewer coordinates can be regarded as a function on the original cube, independent of the unused coordinates. Its weighted coefficient norm SS, the quantity on the left-hand side of (1.4), is therefore bounded by the same MM.

Remark 2.2.

We separate the first eleven levels so that the random-partition argument applies uniformly to the remaining degrees. With our balance interval, r≥12r\geq 12 ensures d,e≥r/6≥2d,e\geq r/6\geq 2; hence qd,qe>1q_{d},q_{e}>1 and both damping factors are positive, so they can be removed at a uniformly bounded cost. The same cutoff gives the common probability bound p=1−2e−8/3p=1-2e^{-8/3} used in the contraction estimate.

Estimating the first eleven levels by Markov’s inequality costs m22m^{22}, and removing the weight r−5r^{-5} costs m5m^{5}. These two contributions give the exponent 2727. For simplicity of the argument, we did not try to optimize the exponent.

3. Application to the Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture

The Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture [12, Conjecture 1.7] asserts that every f:Qn→[−1,1]f:Q_{n}\to[-1,1] of degree at most mm has a coordinate ii with Infi⁡(f)≥c0​(Var⁡(f)/m)C0\operatorname{Inf}_{i}(f)\geq c_{0}(\operatorname{Var}(f)/m)^{C_{0}} for absolute constants c0,C0>0c_{0},C_{0}>0. For coefficients of one common magnitude, the implication from polynomial Bohnenblust–Hille bounds was already noted in [6]; here the magnitude may vary with the degree.

Proof of Corollary 1.3.

Put vr=∑|S|=r|f^​(S)|2=(nr)​ar2v_{r}=\sum_{|S|=r}|\widehat{f}(S)|^{2}=\binom{n}{r}a_{r}^{2}. The hypothesis gives, for every i∈[n]i\in[n],

Var⁡(f)=∑r=1mvr,Infi⁡(f)=∑r=1m(n−1r−1)​ar2=1n​∑r=1mr​vr.\operatorname{Var}(f)=\sum_{r=1}^{m}v_{r},\qquad\operatorname{Inf}_{i}(f)=\sum_{r=1}^{m}\binom{n-1}{r-1}a_{r}^{2}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{m}rv_{r}.

Moreover, since 2/qr=1+1/r2/q_{r}=1+1/r and (nr)≥(n/r)r\binom{n}{r}\geq(n/r)^{r},

𝒮r​(f)2=(nr)1/r​vr≥nr​vr.\mathcal{S}_{r}(f)^{2}=\binom{n}{r}^{1/r}v_{r}\geq\frac{n}{r}\,v_{r}.

Cauchy–Schwarz and Theorem 1.2 therefore yield

Var⁡(f)2\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}(f)^{2} ≤(∑r=1mr​vr)​(∑r=1mvrr)\displaystyle\leq\left(\sum_{r=1}^{m}rv_{r}\right)\left(\sum_{r=1}^{m}\frac{v_{r}}{r}\right)
≤Infi⁡(f)​∑r=1m𝒮r​(f)2\displaystyle\leq\operatorname{Inf}_{i}(f)\sum_{r=1}^{m}\mathcal{S}_{r}(f)^{2}
≤m10​Infi⁡(f)​∑r=1m𝒮r​(f)2r10\displaystyle\leq m^{10}\operatorname{Inf}_{i}(f)\sum_{r=1}^{m}\frac{\mathcal{S}_{r}(f)^{2}}{r^{10}}
≤K2​m54​Infi⁡(f),\displaystyle\leq K^{2}m^{54}\operatorname{Inf}_{i}(f),

where the last step uses ‖f‖∞≤1\|f\|_{\infty}\leq 1. Taking c=K−2c=K^{-2} proves the corollary. ∎

Acknowledgments

P. Ivanisvili was supported in part by NSF grants DMS-2152401 (CAREER) and DMS-2554183, a Simons Fellowship, and a Humboldt Research Fellowship for Experienced Researchers.

The authors acknowledge the use of AI tools, in particular Grok Bots. Following the release of Pellegrino and Teixeira’s paper [9] on polynomial growth of the complex polynomial Bohnenblust–Hille constants, we prompted Grok Bots to use that work as a starting point for proving polynomial bounds on the Hamming cube. Grok Bots generated a proof, which we checked and verified to be correct. Grok’s raw output was publicly circulated the author in an X post on August 27, 2026; see the original draft [11]. The present paper develops that proof into a detailed exposition, with additional explanations to make the argument easier to follow.
